query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-depositing a thin aluminum layer onto the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy surface will promote the in situ formation of a stable, protective alumina-based tribo-film during sliding that maintains low friction and wear from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: An untreated CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix exhibiting moderate oxidation and wear under sliding at various temperatures.
generation.intervention: A thin, uniform aluminum coating (or targeted Al surface doping) applied to the CoCrFeNi substrate prior to sliding tests.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding tests conducted in air over temperatures ranging from 25 °C to 800 °C under representative contact loads (e.g., moderate load levels typical of industrial sliding applications) and sliding speeds where wear and friction are measurable.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, in situ tribo-oxide layer—predominantly alumina (Al2O3) —at the sliding interface that bonds strongly with the HEA matrix.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures the thin Al layer minimally alters surface friction, but as sliding-induced heating occurs, the aluminum reacts with oxygen to form a hard, low-shear tribo-oxide film. This film acts as a protective barrier, reducing direct metal-to-metal contact, suppressing adhesive and abrasive wear, and thereby maintaining a low coefficient of friction across the full temperature regime.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, the Al-treated alloy is expected to show a significantly reduced friction coefficient and lower wear rate consistently from room temperature to 800 °C, with the effect becoming more pronounced at higher sliding temperatures due to enhanced oxide layer formation.
generation.baseline: Sliding performance (friction coefficient and wear rate) of untreated CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy under the same environmental, load, and temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: Test conditions are limited to dry sliding in an oxidizing atmosphere (air) and moderate contact loads; performance may differ under lubricated conditions or in inert atmospheres.
generation.uncertainty: The temperature dependence of oxide layer stability and its detailed wear behavior over the entire 25 °C to 800 °C range introduces uncertainty in the exact degree of performance improvement. In addition, optimizing the aluminum layer thickness for both adhesion and optimal tribo-oxide formation requires further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one set with a pre-deposited thin aluminum coating (using a consistent application process such as physical vapor deposition) and one set left unmodified as baseline. Subject both sets to standardized dry sliding tests in air at multiple fixed temperatures (e.g., 25 °C, 200 °C, 400 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C) under identical loads and sliding speeds.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (continuous monitoring during sliding)
Wear rate (post-test weight loss or wear track volume analysis)
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural characterization (e.g., SEM/EDS, XRD) to confirm formation and integrity of the alumina tribo-film
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in both the friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the baseline CoCrFeNi samples across the full temperature range, or if the protective alumina tribo-film does not form or remains unstable at high temperatures (800 °C), the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Revealing the Interface Characteristic and Bonding Ability of CoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy/Al Composite by First-Principles Calculations

Abstract: AbstractIn this work, the interfacial atomic bonding process and atom-matching structure of Al atoms deposited on the crystal plane of CoCrFeNi HEA were investigated by first-principles calculations. The relevant physical parameters, including crystal structure, lattice constants, chemical bonding, and differential charge distribution, were studied in detail. The results showed that the constructed crystal model of CoCrFeNi HEA has a stable structure, and the binding energy of Al atoms deposited constantly on different crystal planes at different sites is less than −16.21 eV, indicating a strong interface bonding ability. With the increase in deposited atoms, the material is subjected to a phase transition from two-dimensional chemical adsorption of Al atoms in a single layer to three-dimensional chemical binding of the bulk. Furthermore, the electron cloud occurred through the interaction of positive and negative charges at the interface, indicating that the charge has been transferred along with a chemical bond between Al and CoCrFeNi
